name: Fenugreek

lead: Fenugreek is a Mediterranean and South Asian plant whose seeds are used as a spice and in traditional medicine. In fitness circles it is sold as a natural testosterone booster, usually as seed extract capsules, taken by lifters hoping for better training results, libido and a leaner, more muscular physique.

The chain: seed compounds such as steroidal saponins are proposed to nudge testosterone, which supports training and body composition. A few small randomised trials of specific extracts, and meta-analyses of them, report higher total testosterone or sexual-function scores in some men. Reviewers note few studies, varied extracts and small samples, and human mechanistic data are limited.

paras: It is taken as seed extract capsules or powder, often inside multi-herb men's-health products and paired with training. Users report effects, if any, over weeks.

Reported side effects include diarrhea, bloating and gas, and a maple-like body odor. It may lower blood sugar and interfere with anticoagulants and diabetes drugs, and it is not considered safe in pregnancy. It is sold as a dietary supplement in the US, not an approved drug.

angle.text: Fenugreek seed extract is sold as a natural testosterone and libido supplement, taken by lifters hoping for better training results and body composition. Small trials of branded extracts report modest hormone changes in some men.

lead: Fenugreek (Trigonella foenum-graecum) is an annual legume native to the Near East and Mediterranean whose seeds and leaves are widely used as a spice and herb, particularly in South Asian cooking [1]. It has a long history in traditional medicine, including documented use in ancient Egypt and Greek and Indian medicine [2].

In appearance-focused and fitness communities, fenugreek seed extract is discussed as an herbal "testosterone booster" and libido aid, and is a common ingredient in multi-herb men's-health products [3][4].

Several small randomized trials of specific extracts, and meta-analyses pooling them, have reported higher total testosterone or improved sexual-function scores in some men; systematic reviews describe these findings as limited by few trials, differing extracts and small samples [5]. Wikipedia states that no high-quality evidence supports therapeutic properties and that the US FDA has not approved fenugreek for clinical use [1].
infobox: Spice; traditional galactagogue; supplement for testosterone, blood sugar [1][2]
Dietary supplement / food (US); not an approved drug [1]

paras: Culinary use is the most common: seeds are roasted or ground in curries, pickles and spice blends, and leaves are eaten as a vegetable [1]. Traditional medicine has used it as a digestive aid, to support milk production and for menstrual cramps [1][2].

subs.h: Use in appearance and fitness communities
paras: In men's health and sports nutrition, standardized seed extracts are sold alone or with ashwagandha, tribulus, tongkat ali and other herbs for testosterone, libido and training support [2][4]. A US homeopathic-labelled product on DailyMed lists fenugreek among its ingredients and is marketed as supporting testosterone output [4].

A 2020 meta-analysis of four clinical trials in men reported that fenugreek extract had a significant effect on total serum testosterone [5]. A 2016 double-blind placebo-controlled trial of 120 men aged 43 to 70 found that a 12-week course of the branded extract Testofen was associated with lower androgen-deficiency symptom scores, better sexual-function scores and higher total and free testosterone than placebo [5].

A 2021 systematic review of 32 studies on 13 herbs found that fenugreek seed extract and ashwagandha root extract showed positive effects on testosterone in men, but concluded that evidence is limited by few studies per herb, varied extracts and doses, and small samples [5]. A 2023 systematic review of six randomized trials on muscle performance found that four reported gains in strength, endurance or lean mass with fenugreek glycoside or saponin preparations, while two small trials of fewer than ten participants examined glycogen resynthesis; its authors noted doping rules and possible liver and kidney effects [5].

ClinicalTrials.gov lists a completed trial of fenugreek supplementation in men with testosterone deficiency (n=58) and trials in diabetes, lactation, polycystic ovary syndrome and obesity [6]. Studies of blood-sugar effects are described by Wikipedia as of limited quality [1].
Reported side effects include diarrhea, bloating, gas and sweating, and a maple-like odor of sweat, urine or breast milk. People allergic to peanuts or chickpeas may react [1].

Fenugreek may lower blood sugar and so interact with antidiabetic drugs, and its coumarin-like compounds may affect anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs; reviews of herb-drug interactions have discussed warfarin and analgesic interactions [1][7][8]. Wikipedia states fenugreek is not safe during pregnancy because of possible effects on uterine contractions, and may be unsafe for women with hormone-sensitive cancers [1]. Sprouts from a seed lot imported from Egypt were suspected in the 2011 E. coli O104:H4 outbreak in Europe [1].

Seeds contain steroidal saponins including diosgenin, a precursor used in pharmaceutical steroid synthesis, along with fiber, galactomannan and the alkaloid trigonelline [2][9][10]. Proposed mechanisms for testosterone-related effects (for example, effects on enzymes that convert androgens to estrogens) come mainly from laboratory work; research on trigonelline and diosgenin has focused on diabetes and cancer models [9][10].

Charred seeds have been found at an archaeological site in Iraq dated to about 4000 BC and in Tutankhamun's tomb, and Roman writers described its use as fodder and wine flavoring [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, places its earliest medical documentation in the Ebers Papyrus [2].

Fenugreek is sold in the US as a dietary supplement. Forum users on looksmax.org have asked whether it is worth taking for testosterone or libido, with replies ranging from personal reports of improved lifts to suspicion that it is a "cope" [3].
